item.title: Triadic energy routes in a short laminar separation bubble
item.description: arXiv:2610.27035v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The kinetic energy budget of a laminar separation bubble on a compressor blade is formed mode by mode in frequency and spanwise wavenumber from a direct numerical simulation at a Reynolds number of $2.5\times10^{5}$ based on the axial chord. The nonlinear transfer between modes is evaluated as a triadic tensor that gives the energy exchanged in every triad, the roles of its three modes, and the location of the exchange. Nine dominant tonal modes are identified: the flapping of the bubble, the Kelvin-Helmholtz mode with its sidebands, a pair of modes near reattachment, and their sum, difference, and harmonic. They hold 8% of the fluctuation energy, and their triads are responsible for 19% of the energy exchanged. Every tonal mode is fed by the mean shear and exports 69 to 82% of the energy it takes from the mean flow. The Kelvin-Helmholtz mode sends 45% of the energy it sheds to lower frequencies. The largest of these transfers is a triad in which it acts as a catalyst. The exchange in each triad is split into nine channels by velocity components. In every triad of spanwise-uniform modes, one channel dominates: the wall-tangential velocity of the donor advected by the wall-normal velocity of the catalyst. For a pair of oblique modes, the same advection by the two-dimensional Kelvin-Helmholtz mode exchanges their spanwise velocity, which the mean flow cannot produce. The rollers thus become three-dimensional through the advecting velocity of the Kelvin-Helmholtz mode, which supplies no energy to the exchange.
item.dc:creator: Gustavo Lopes, Pawel Przytarski, Daniele Simoni, Davide Lengani

item.title: A Neural Implicit Flow Super-Resolution Approach for Reacting Flows
item.description: arXiv:2610.27215v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a novel framework for reconstructing fine-resolution scalar fields from coarse-resolution data in 2D unsteady flames using an extension of neural implicit flow (NIF). The framework leverages the novel architecture of NIF to develop an efficient representation of scalar fields in spatio-temporal reacting flows. Different strategies are adopted within the proposed framework to establish super-resolution for multiscalar fields in combustion. They include 1) a reconfiguration of the input and output fields, 2) the use of a latent composition space based on nonlinear principal component analysis (NLPCA) to reconstruct the fine-resolution fields, and the conversion from nonlinear principal components (NLPCs) to species and temperature contours, and 3) the adoption of multiple ParameterNets in the NIF architecture, each accommodating one of the NLPCs. The framework was validated on a 2D unsteady Bunsen-stabilized lean premixed methane-air flame with forcing at the inlet. The results, using a coarsening ratio of 8 in a given direction, show that the adoption of multiple ParameterNets yields more accurate super-resolution than a single ParameterNet without any additional cost in the hyperparameters.
item.dc:creator: Dakshaka Vishwajith Amarathunga, Lanre M. Oshinowo, Ji-Woong Park, Tarek Echekki

item.title: Fully resolved particle dynamics over long time scales in acoustofluidic flows: Theory and numerical simulations
item.description: arXiv:2610.27228v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a perturbation-based theoretical framework, together with its immersed boundary/volume penalization implementation, for long-time simulations of fully resolved rigid-particle dynamics in acoustically actuated flows. A perturbation formulation separates the fast acoustic time scale from the slow mean dynamics, avoiding long-time direct integration of the fully compressible Navier-Stokes equations. The immersed rigid body is represented through a Brinkman penalization term in equations posed over a unified fluid-solid domain. The coupled fluid-particle system is decomposed into a time-harmonic first-order problem governing the acoustic response and a time-averaged second-order problem. A central challenge in this decomposition is the treatment of the moving fluid-solid interface. We derive order-consistent expressions for the structural velocities, comprising rigid-body and Stokes-drift contributions, and formulate the corresponding first- and second-order rigid-body equations of motion. For a circular particle in two dimensions, the simulations reveal substantial differences in the magnitude and structure of acoustic streaming around fixed and freely moving particles, highlighting the importance of two-way fluid-structure coupling. The results also show that particle-density effects are more complex than suggested by simplified descriptions based solely on the acoustic contrast factor. The framework captures the mean particle dynamics using time steps associated with the slow particle-motion scale rather than the much smaller acoustic time scale. Finally, simulations of an elliptical particle demonstrate the ability of the method to capture coupled translational and rotational motion. The proposed approach therefore provides an efficient route to fully resolved, long-time simulations of acoustically driven rigid-particle motion while retaining two-way fluid-structure coupling.
item.dc:creator: Khemraj Gautam Kshetri, Amneet Pal Singh Bhalla, Nitesh Nama

item.title: NeRF-Inspired Neural Fields for 3D Super-resolution of Reacting-Flows
item.description: arXiv:2610.27284v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The multiscale nature of turbulent reacting flows and the importance of fine-scale structures pose challenges for super-resolution. We investigate a 3D super-resolution framework inspired by Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF), called Neural Field Super-Resolution (NFSR), to reconstruct fine-resolution fields from coarsened reacting-flow fields. The proposed formulation adapts the continuous coordinate-conditioned representation of NeRF to physical flow-field reconstruction by conditioning spatial coordinates with local coarse-grid thermochemical information, while eliminating radiance prediction and volume rendering. Principal component analysis is used to provide a compact and low-dimensional representation of the thermochemical state, and a hierarchical extension, H-NFSR, progressively reconstructs the solution through intermediate resolution levels. The framework is evaluated using three-dimensional direct numerical simulation data for a turbulent premixed hydrogen-air flame, with an overall spatial coarsening factor of eight in each coordinate direction. The results demonstrate consistently better prediction measures and a higher ability to reconstruct fine-scale information than tricubic interpolation on the unseen test realization. The hierarchical formulation reduces visible coarse-cell imprinting. In contrast, biased sampling mainly benefits the most localized structures. Three-dimensional isosurface comparisons further show that H-NFSR recovers much of the small and intermediate features of the flow, including surface wrinkling and local flame curvature effects. These results highlight the potential of coordinate-conditioned neural fields as a flexible framework for three-dimensional coarse-to-fine reconstruction of reacting-flow simulations.
item.dc:creator: Dakshaka Vishwajith Amarathunga, Shang-Ru Li, Tarek Echekki

item.title: Formation of a Vorticity Singularity in an Axisymmetric Poloidal Flow
item.description: arXiv:2610.27330v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this work, building on previous studies of plane-parallel flows, we investigate the rapid growth of the frozen-in vorticity field in an axisymmetric poloidal flow. We present the results of numerical simulations performed using supercomputing resources. We show that exponentially growing velocity gradients can develop on the axis of symmetry, while vorticity gradients grow superexponentially. These results are qualitatively similar to those previously obtained for vorticity in a simpler two-dimensional flow.
item.dc:creator: Evgeny Kuznetsov, Evgeny Mikhailov, Mikhail Serdukov

item.title: Predicting trigger in streak breakdown via Picard-Chebyshev approach in plane-Poiseuille flow
item.description: arXiv:2610.27475v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The evolution of finite-amplitude disturbances is critical in the prediction of laminar-to-turbulent transition. To analyze the transient growth of disturbances, Pralits et al. (J. Fluid Mechanics, 2015) proposed a weakly nonlinear optimal perturbation (WNLOP) analysis that accounts for the effect of mean-flow distortion on the fundamental wave. The present study formulates a WNLOP analysis via Picard--Chebyshev iteration for compressible parallel flows to predict streak breakdown. The formulation incorporates the non-modal amplification of disturbances and their nonlinear interactions for polychromatic waves, considering all the possible nonlinear interactions starting from a finite set of initial wavenumber components. The nonlinear interaction is tracked as a monotonically increasing set of wavenumber components; specifically, the first-order approximation recovers the linear disturbance equation, the third-order approximation corresponds to the amplitude equation of weakly nonlinear theory, and further iterations systematically approach DNS results in the weakly nonlinear regime. By applying the proposed formulation to a subcritical plane Poiseuille flow at Mach number $\mathrm{M}=0.3$ and Reynolds number $\mathrm{Re}=3000$, the proposed formulation demonstrates high predictive accuracy in comparison with DNS calculations and succeeds in identifying the optimal perturbation restricted to a planar wave that causes streak breakdown in full nonlinear simulation. The proposed method predicts the nonlinear interaction between the streak and the planar wave, which generates an oblique wave and subsequent harmonic waves characterized by an alternating streamwise vortex structure, whose amplitude determines whether further nonlinear interactions are induced to trigger the turbulent transition.
item.dc:creator: Nobutaka Taniguchi, Aiko Yakeno

item.title: Influence of Ideal, Cubic, and Multiparameter Helmholtz Equations of State on the Static and Dynamic Performance of Porous Aerostatic Journal Bearings
item.description: arXiv:2610.27840v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Porous aerostatic gas bearings are commonly modeled using the ideal-gas law, although non-ideal thermodynamic behavior may become relevant for alternative working fluids. This study quantifies the influence of the thermodynamic closure on the stationary and dynamic response of porous aerostatic journal bearings. A finite-volume formulation couples the compressible Reynolds equation with three-dimensional Darcy flow, retaining transient gas storage in both domains. Density is used as the primary thermodynamic variable, allowing the ideal-gas, van der Waals, Soave--Redlich--Kwong, Peng--Robinson, and multiparameter Helmholtz equations of state to be evaluated within an otherwise unchanged bearing model. Air, R1234yf, and R1234ze(E) are considered. For air, EOS-induced differences remain negligible over the investigated range. For the refrigerants, the ideal-gas approximation produces several-percent deviations, with supplied mass flow and dynamic force response being particularly sensitive. The cubic equations substantially reduce these deviations, with the employed Peng--Robinson formulation providing the closest agreement with the Helmholtz reference for both refrigerants at a computational cost comparable to the other cubic models. The results identify density and differential compressibility as the main thermodynamic quantities governing the propagation of EOS errors into mass transport and transient gas storage.
item.dc:creator: Laurenz Stellmach, Steffen Nitzschke, Elmar Woschke

item.title: Second-order difference-frequency effects on floating wind turbine responses: full-QTF modelling and experimental comparison
item.description: arXiv:2610.27940v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accurate prediction of low-frequency responses is important for the dynamic assessment of floating offshore wind turbines (FOWTs), as second-order difference-frequency wave loads can contribute substantially to platform motions and mooring loads. Their relative importance, however, remains less well established when aerodynamic and hydrodynamic low-frequency excitations coexist under operating conditions. This study develops an efficient time-domain formulation for full difference-frequency quadratic transfer function (QTF) loading using bandwidth truncation and integrates it into a fully coupled model of the IEA 15 MW turbine on the VolturnUS-S semi-submersible platform. Numerical predictions are compared with 1:70-scale real-time hybrid wave-basin experiments covering both irregular wave-only and combined turbulent wind-wave conditions. Three hydrodynamic formulations are compared: linear wave excitation, Newman's approximation, and the full-QTF model. Under wave-only conditions, second-order difference-frequency loading substantially improves the prediction of surge and the associated mooring response, particularly in energetic sea states, with the full-QTF model generally providing the closest agreement with measured low-frequency spectra and peak-amplitude distributions. Under combined wind-wave conditions, low-frequency thrust fluctuations dominate near rated wind speed, reducing the relative importance of difference-frequency wave excitation, whereas its contribution becomes more apparent at higher wind speeds as thrust fluctuations diminish. Overall, the full-QTF model provides the most consistent improvement over the linear and Newman models, with maximum surge standard deviation discrepancy from measurement under the most energetic wave conditions less than 18%, with smaller discrepancies for heave, pitch, and mooring tensions.
item.dc:creator: Yi Zhang, Tom Tosdevin, Tianning Tang, Peter Stansby

item.title: Spatially developing drag reduction across a finite oscillating wall
item.description: arXiv:2610.28104v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The spatial evolution of a turbulent boundary layer at $Re_\tau = 652$ developing across a finite spanwise oscillating wall is investigated with normalised oscillation period of $T^+ \approx 101$ and amplitude $A^+ \approx 7$, yielding a drag reduction of 32\%. The spatial distribution of skin friction is estimated adopting a recently introduced near-wall data nonlinear regression method based on the arctangent function, which circumvents the requirement of high wall-normal resolution to capture the viscous sublayer. The method viability is assessed against reference DNS data, and the trends of measurement errors from experimental data are well reproduced. The local impact of the control action is examined by evaluating the spatial development of scalar fields of turbulence statistics as well as conditional quadrant analysis to link the onset and recovery transients to turbulence events. The boundary layer response is observed to follow an exponential decay law for the skin friction spatial evolution. The decay length-scale corresponds to $0.6$ boundary layer thicknesses $\delta$ for the onset transient and $0.9\delta$ for the recovery one. The same exponential fit applied to the Reynolds stresses yields a response within $0.5\delta$, with the exception of the shear stress peak, that requires a significantly longer distance.
item.dc:creator: Marco Galli, Nicol\`o Scaiola, Ferdinand F. J. Schrijer, Fulvio Scarano

item.title: Wavepackets in subsonic elliptical jets: coherent-structure eduction and linear modelling
item.description: arXiv:2610.28221v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study coherent structures extracted from time-resolved particle image velocimetry (TR-PIV) measurements of isothermal elliptical jets with aspect ratio of 1:2, at Mach numbers 0.4 and 0.7. The velocity snapshots are decomposed according to the D$_2$ symmetry. Spectral proper orthogonal decomposition (SPOD) is then used to identify coherent structures. Modelling is performed using three-dimensional parabolised stability equations (3D-PSE) based on linearisation about the time-averaged mean flows. A comparison between SPOD and 3D-PSE results shows alignment of SPOD and single-mode PSE structures of up to 70\%. A linear combination of PSE solutions, obtained from the family of initially unstable local modes, leads to SPOD-PSE alignment of up to 90\%. Limitations are observed at low frequencies and near the nozzle and are attributed to the existence of non-modal amplification mechanisms. The study shows that coherent structures in turbulent elliptical jets can be educed using the D$_2$-SPOD approach, and modelled using 3D PSE.
item.dc:creator: Filipe Ramos do Amaral, Mateus Peixoto Avanci, Jean-Christophe Robinet, Peter Jordan, J\'er\^ome Huber, Gr\'egoire Pont

item.title: Exponential Growth of Turbulent Cross Helicity in Shear-Flow-Driven Turbulence
item.description: arXiv:2610.28424v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cross helicity, the velocity--magnetic-field correlation, is an ideal invariant of incompressible magnetohydrodynamics and constrains energy cascades and magnetic-field generation. Although cross helicity typically decays via visco-resistive effects, we analytically demonstrate that it grows exponentially in sheared inhomogeneous turbulence. This cross-helical shear instability is confirmed using three-dimensional numerical simulations. Growth requires a nonzero gradient of the Reynolds--Maxwell stress to produce turbulent cross helicity; this production overcomes effective losses when shear exceeds a threshold set by the ratio of turbulent magnetic to momentum diffusivities.
item.dc:creator: B. Tripathi, A. E. Fraser, P. W. Terry, E. G. Zweibel, M. J. Pueschel, A. M. Beloborodov

item.title: Reduced graph-based representations of detonation-containing flows
item.description: arXiv:2610.28486v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A graph neural network (GNN)-based autoencoder is leveraged to produce reduced latent graph representations of detonation-containing flows. In a two-dimensional hydrogen-air channel configuration with a uniform fuel-air mixture, it was found that latent graphs with effective resolutions of twice the induction length are capable of reconstructing both the wavefront and the post-shock region of the cellular detonation wave structure. Extrapolation studies using stratified and three-dimensional detonation configurations revealed an intrinsic property of GNN-based reconstruction from reduced latent graphs -- a representational hierarchy, rooted in the local nature of message passing, that tends to prioritize features at the detonation front (i.e., the wavefront profile and triple points) over the downstream deflagrative regions. In particular, it was found that at a fixed ambient condition, the information contained in uniform two-dimensional detonations was sufficient to reconstruct the wavefront structure of both stratified and three-dimensional detonations. Overall, this work demonstrates the utility of GNNs for both reduction and information overlap extraction in detonation-containing flows, opening promising pathways for accelerated simulations of these flows.
item.dc:creator: Sinaendhran Pujali Elilarasan, Michael Ullman, Shivam Barwey

item.title: Matrix-Free Resolvent Analysis for Large-Scale Aerodynamic Systems
item.description: arXiv:2610.26931v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: At industrial scale the cost of resolvent analysis is set by the linear solves and the assembly and storage of the Jacobian. We present a matrix-free resolvent framework in the Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes solver ADflow: automatic differentiation supplies the action of the shifted Jacobian and its Hermitian transpose, preconditioned Krylov solves recycle subspaces across a Lanczos bidiagonalization, and every gain is certified by a backward error. It is applied to the NASA Common Research Model wing at Mach 0.85 and 4.2 degrees on three grid levels of 0.45, 3.6 and 28.8 million cells, the finest with 1.73x10^8 complex unknowns, 2.3 times the largest reported resolvent computation. On the coarsest level an unstable buffet mode makes the gain peak a resonance; on the finer two the operator is stable and the peak, 1.33x10^4 at omega = 6.4 and 3.0x10^3 near omega = 7.7, is a pseudo-resonance of damped modes whose buffet cells travel outboard at about 0.3 times the free-stream speed. Refinement turns an oscillator into an amplifier of the same mechanism, as forced simulations confirm. A certified frequency costs 3.6 minutes on 128 cores at 2.7 million unknowns, with 14 to 34 kB per unknown, nearly four orders of magnitude below a sparse factorization.
item.dc:creator: Rohit Sunil Kanchi, Sicheng He

item.title: Load-Balanced Neural-Network-Aided Adaptive Tabulation of Phase Equilibria for Transcritical Multiphase Flows
item.description: arXiv:2610.26984v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Simulating high-pressure transcritical flows with phase change is critical for advanced propulsion, yet traditional first-principles approaches, vapor-liquid equilibrium (VLE) calculations, consume most of the runtime and frequently fail to converge. Standalone machine learning models introduce heavy evaluation overhead across large grids, while dynamic tabulation still relies on fragile iterative solvers. To resolve these limitations, this study introduces a hybrid In-Situ Adaptive Tabulation and Artificial Neural Network (ISAT-ANN) framework. A pre-trained ANN replaces the iterative solver during table expansion to guarantee crash-free operation, while ISAT enables rapid data retrieval via local linear interpolation. To eliminate parallel load imbalances, an O(N) greedy load-balancing algorithm redistributes computational tasks across cores. Coupled with Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR), the framework was validated on a Mach 5 shock-droplet interaction benchmark. It accurately captured shock-interface dynamics without instability, achieving a 2.30 times speedup in thermodynamic calculations on a single core and 2.62 times in parallel over standalone ANNs, with AMR providing an additional 2.92 times overall efficiency boost. This plug-and-play framework offers a stable, scalable path for high-fidelity multiphase flow simulations.
item.dc:creator: Navneeth Srinivasan, Po-Yu Lai, Suo Yang

item.title: Synthetic Dataset Generation, Physical Consistency and Active Learning for Shape-Informed Surrogate Modeling of Hemodynamics
item.description: arXiv:2610.27130v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Model order reduction has the potential to enable real-time patient-specific assessment of cardiovascular flows. However, it still faces significant challenges stemming from the geometric variability of vascular anatomies. Building upon the SynthAorta dataset (Bosnjak et al., IEEE Trans. Med. Imag. 45(1), 2026) of physiological aortic geometries, we generate an extensive dataset of physiologically consistent computational fluid dynamics solutions through an automatic boundary-condition adjustment procedure. A common reference geometry allows all patient-specific anatomies to be represented by displacement fields, providing point-to-point correspondence without the need for geometric registration. Based on this dataset, we develop Graph U-Net and Transformer U-Net surrogate models to predict velocity and pressure fields at peak systole. We further investigate two strategies to enhance data efficiency and prediction accuracy: active learning and differentiable physical consistency constraints based on the finite element residual. The results show that active learning is strongly regime-dependent: while it offers little benefit over random sampling during early training, it improves performance during fine-tuning through gradient- and subspace-based acquisition strategies. Similarly, physical consistency constraints prove to be substantially more effective as a fine-tuning objective than as a regularizer applied throughout training. Finally, out-of-distribution studies demonstrate that the primary limitation of surrogate models lies in the geometric support of the underlying parametrization rather than in the neural network architectures themselves. The proposed framework combines synthetic dataset generation, geometry-aware surrogate modeling, physics-informed optimization, and active learning into a scalable workflow for inter-patient hemodynamic prediction.
item.dc:creator: Francesco Romor, Richard Schussnig, Charles A. Taylor, Gerhard A. Holzapfel, Alfonso Caiazzo

item.title: Neural Operator Splitting for Fluid Dynamics in Complex Geometry
item.description: arXiv:2610.27671v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Solving dynamical systems in complex and diverse geometries remains challenging for both numerical solvers and learning-based surrogate models. We propose Neural Operator Splitting, a framework for learning fluid dynamics while preserving the physical structure of fractional-step numerical schemes. Instead of learning the full-step evolution monolithically, we decompose each time step into physically interpretable steps, and learn each operator separately using intermediate states from the underlying numerical solver. Guided by the linearity properties of the fractional steps, we introduce a conditional-linear Fourier neural operator (CL-FNO) whose linear state mappings are modulated by nonlinear conditioning on inputs such as boundary geometry. We further introduce two complementary strategies, symmetry sampling and corrective cycling, to mitigate error accumulation during autoregressive rollout. Experiments on 2D and 3D fluid flows with varying geometries and initial conditions show that our full model reduces mean relative $L^2$ rollout error by 68\% in 2D and 40\% in 3D compared with a single full-step neural operator. At comparable error levels, neural-operator inference is approximately $10^3$ times faster per step than the Monte Carlo solver.
item.dc:creator: Jianxiang Li, Xi Deng, Hong Chul Nam, Anima Anandkumar

item.title: DeHNSSo-v2: A compressible, curvilinear, and efficient extension of the Delft Harmonic Navier-Stokes Solver
item.description: arXiv:2610.27906v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We present DeHNSSo-v2, a major update of DeHNSSo-v1 (Westerbeek et al., Comput. Phys. Commun. 302, 2024), the open-source Delft Harmonic Navier-Stokes Solver for nonlinear stability analysis of shear flows. The new release adds a compressible formulation on general two-dimensional body-fitted geometries, automatic grid generation, linear-cost sparse assembly, reusable per-mode factorizations, and Newton pseudo-arclength continuation for high-amplitude nonlinear solutions. The curvilinear formulation preserves the fourth-order accuracy of the discretization on strongly distorted grids, and the compressible solver is confirmed to reproduce DeHNSSo-v1 in the incompressible limit. Validation spans published benchmarks for linear instability of compressible flat-plate boundary layers from $\mathrm{Ma}=0.5$ to $\mathrm{Ma}=4.5$, nonlinear oblique-mode breakdown at $\mathrm{Ma}=1.6$, nonlinear swept-wing crossflow compared with direct numerical simulations, and linear Tollmien-Schlichting wave interaction with a modeled surface-embedded Helmholtz resonator compared with experimentally validated linearized Navier-Stokes simulations. On the nonlinear test cases of DeHNSSo-v1, the computational developments result in a speed-up of approximately one order of magnitude. By broadening the scope and reducing the cost of DeHNSSo-v1, DeHNSSo-v2 provides the boundary-layer-transition and flow-control community with an accessible tool for studying receptivity, nonlinear disturbance evolution, and instability interactions with complex surface geometry and metamaterials across compressibility regimes.
item.dc:creator: Pietro Carlo Boldini, Yifu Chen, Marios Kotsonis

item.title: Dramatic pressure-induced slowdown and the soft glassy rheology of water at 2D material interface
item.description: arXiv:2610.28254v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The flow of molecularly confined water has attracted considerable interest in recent years. Yet despite their exquisite character, current nanofluidic devices cannot probe molecular water flow beyond the linear-response regime, while nanomechanical force- based approaches have produced markedly inconsistent results. Here, using tuning- fork-based atomic force microscopy, we tackle these limitations by measuring the full linear-to-nonlinear, shear-dependent viscoelastic rheology of molecularly confined water at various two-dimensional material interfaces -- demonstrating pronounced rate effects in water flow response. The observed rheological behaviors are remarkably analogous to that of macroscopic soft glassy yielding materials and fully captured by a non-linear model accounting for the shear-induced acceleration of the dynamics -- a hallmark of disordered supercooled and metastable systems. We further unveil a pronounced pressure-induced slowdown in nanoconfined water dynamics, with relaxation times extending into the microsecond range and marked material dependence. These results reveal non-linear, glassy rheology as a general feature of interfacial water and offer a route to tunable, non-linear nanofluidic elements.
item.dc:creator: Guilhem Mariette, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Jean Comtet

item.title: Connecting the Hydrodynamics of Polymeric Fluids and Active Nematics
item.description: arXiv:2601.08296v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We establish a correspondence between the continuum descriptions of polymer solutions and active nematics, two seemingly disparate but well-studied complex fluids. Through a mapping of the governing equations, we demonstrate that polymeric fluids can be interpreted as deformable, contractile, high-temperature active nematics, with an effective activity controlled by polymer extension. Using numerical simulations under Kolmogorov flow, we construct a phase diagram connecting the nematic and polymer limits, highlighting how their one- and two-dimensional instabilities depend on deformability. This encompasses both a flow-suppressed regime, in which active stresses oppose the imposed flow, and a transverse instability that generates secondary flows and leads towards elastic turbulence. The transverse instability is facilitated by spatial gradients in activity, which arise naturally in extensible polymers through variations in chain extension. We further show that the transition into the well-known traveling arrowhead structures in elastic turbulence is marked by the emergence of charge $\pm 1/2$ topological defects in the polymer director field, indicating emergent nematic ordering of stretched polymers. Our results establish a unified framework connecting polymer and active matter hydrodynamics, with implications for low-Reynolds-number turbulence, active polymer systems, and the mechanics of deformable living matter.
item.dc:creator: Vedad Dzanic, Sumesh P. Thampi, Rahil N. Valani, Julia M. Yeomans

item.title: Interface-dominated sliding compound drops
item.description: arXiv:2603.26601v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We investigate compound drops composed of two immiscible nonvolatile partially wetting liquids that slide down an inclined homogeneous smooth solid substrate based on a mesoscopic hydrodynamic two-layer model in full-curvature formulation. First, we briefly investigate the reference case of a liquid drop that stationarily slides on a liquid layer representing an adaptive substrate. Subsequently, we focus on sliding compound drops employing a parameter study to identify qualitative transitions between different drop configurations and time-periodic behavior as well as the underlying bifurcation structure. After analyzing the dependence of drop velocities and dynamic Young and Neumann angles on driving force, also the influence of the ratios of drop volumes and viscosities is briefly considered. An accompanying discussion of the lateral dissipation profile is used to explain the encountered dependence of drop velocity on their configuration. Finally, we consider the time-periodic fusion-overtaking-splitting behavior found outside the existence range of the stationary sliding compound drops.
item.dc:creator: Dominik Thy, Jan Diekmann, Uwe Thiele

item.title: Edge turbulence controlled by topologically self-optimized fluxes in fusion devices
item.description: arXiv:2603.28633v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The magnetic field topology undergoes a drastic transition near the separatrix in magnetic confinement fusion devices, inducing topological chaos. This phenomenon is investigated across tokamaks, stellarators, and the RFX-mod reversed-field pinch. Within this boundary region, self-optimized fluxes of shear-generated magnetic and cross-helicity, together with the ensemble-averaged magnetic moment, are hypothesized to govern plasma stability, self-organization, and transport. By treating the averaged magnetic moment as an active scalar and using the Fokker-Planck equation to reconcile kinetic and fluid descriptions, this study couples its dynamics with a novel multichannel, self-optimized helicity cascade loop. The derived spectral laws for the floating potential and ion saturation current agree with measurements from numerous experiments. Distributed chaos theory quantifies the randomness of the observed states, revealing that a narrow layer at the separatrix suppresses strong core randomness, transforming it into distributed chaos in the scrape-off layer. A constrained variational principle for active control has also been considered. Tuning Lagrangian multipliers via helicity injection drives the system toward an attractor state that stabilizes the separatrix shear layer, suppresses edge-localized modes, and spreads the heat load, using magnetic reconnection as a nonlinear solver. This framework circumvents conventional diffusive limitations, providing an analytical foundation to model heat-load patterns and stochastic ripple loss in next-step devices.
item.dc:creator: A. Bershadskii

item.title: Quantifying Injection-Driven Interphase Mass Transfer within Porous Media via Time-Elapsed X-ray micro-Computed Tomography
item.description: arXiv:2604.07743v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Understanding interphase mass transfer is essential for a variety of applications in porous media, from groundwater remediation to geologic energy storage. While X-ray micro-Computed Tomography (micro-CT) is a measurement technique that can provide critical in situ observations, quantifying transient mass transfer requires models and workflows capable of compensating for the spatial and temporal resolution constraints. Current literature presents three analytical frameworks for evaluating interphase mass transfer using time-lapsed sequences of X-ray micro-CT scans: the Slice-Averaged Concentration approach, the Non-Classified per-Cluster approach, and the Classified per-Cluster approach. We systematically evaluate the frameworks and results for each of the three approaches as applied to several sequences of time-lapsed scans, each observing hydrogen dissolution experiments at varying injection rates. Estimates of average mass transfer coefficients vary within an order of magnitude, increasing as injection rate decreases. However, approach estimates diverged when approximating more complex, pore-scale phenomena, such as aqueous solute concentration. Per-Cluster approaches preserve more information, enabling quantification of important localized physicochemical processes such as dissolution fingering and cluster remobilization. Given the lack of ground-truth benchmarks for mass-transfer kinetic data in the conditions of interest to fields such as geologic storage, additional research is still needed to understand how these approaches vary under different state and flow conditions. The utility of one approach over another is ultimately determined by the desired level of system detail, at the cost of the computational resources required to achieve it. Our results provide a framework for researchers to select analytical approaches based on the desired level of physical detail.
item.dc:creator: Christopher A. Allison, Ruotong Huang, Anindityo Patmonoaji, Lydia Knuefing, Anna L. Herring

item.title: A high-fidelity numerical database for free-stream-turbulence-induced transition under varying pressure gradients
item.description: arXiv:2606.20139v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Free-stream-turbulence-induced transition under streamwise-varying pressure gradients, as encountered on turbine blades, has received much less attention in high-fidelity simulations than its zero-pressure-gradient counterpart. The ERCOFTAC T3 experiments provide a carefully documented reference for this problem and remain central to transition-model calibration. Complementing them with full-field, three-dimensional data opens new opportunities for the development of physics-based and machine-learning transition models. To this end, wall-resolved implicit large-eddy simulations of the T3A, T3B, and T3C2--C5 flat-plate cases are performed with a high-order compressible solver, using an upstream slip-wall block that lets the synthetic free-stream turbulence develop up to the leading edge. The simulations reproduce well the measured transition locations, integral quantities, and velocity profiles, and predict a separation bubble near the end of the plate for the lowest-Reynolds-number case T3C4. As the Reynolds number decreases and transition moves into the adverse-pressure-gradient region, the mechanism evolves continuously from classical bypass transition to transition governed by the tendency of the laminar boundary layer to separate, up to separation-induced transition. Intermittency, conditioned statistics, and Reynolds-stress budgets document this evolution and the associated non-equilibrium effects, which challenge current RANS transition models.
item.dc:creator: Louenas Zemmour, Xavier Gloerfelt, Paola Cinnella

item.title: Inelastic spreading of viscoelastic drops
item.description: arXiv:2608.10851v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: When a liquid drop impacts a solid surface, rebound and splashing are known to be suppressed by additives that induce elastic effects; however, the influence of elasticity on the maximum spreading radius remains debated. The difficulty lies in isolating elastic resistance from the enhanced spreading caused by viscous shear thinning. Here, we experimentally decouple these effects by investigating Boger fluid drops (constant-viscosity solutions with high elasticity) of polyethylene oxide (PEO) and polyacrylamide (PAAM). We demonstrate that elastic properties do not alter the maximum spreading ratio, even at high concentrations up to 1000 ppm. We formulate an energy balance that accounts for the inertial, capillary, viscous, and elastic contributions, and yields a dimensionless criterion ($\Gamma$) that estimates the degree of elastic effects. We show that $\Gamma \ll 1$ for all impact conditions tested, demonstrating that elastic effects are energetically negligible during droplet spreading, opposite to what Weissenberg and Deborah numbers would predict.
item.dc:creator: Mete Abbot, Thijs Varkevisser, Manglesh Singh, Antoine Gaillard, Devranjan Samanta, Daniel Bonn

item.title: CuAD: Source-to-Source Automatic Differentiation of CUDA Kernels for Discrete Adjoints in Computational Fluid Dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2610.26694v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Discrete adjoint methods give the sensitivities that aerodynamic design and data assimilation require, but they remain hard to obtain for flow solvers that run on graphics processors. This paper presents CuAD, a source-to-source automatic differentiation tool that reads CUDA kernels and writes their tangent and adjoint versions as ordinary CUDA source. Its reverse mode is organised around the GPU thread. It adopts the convention of CUDA kernels that inputs and outputs do not alias, recomputes intermediate values instead of storing them, differentiates pure accumulations without a tape and keeps any remaining tape in a fixed thread-local array. We evaluate CuAD on four kernels from simple flow models and on a two-dimensional Euler solver. All generated derivatives pass dot-product tests to round-off, and the adjoint kernels cost two to six times the primal kernels. On a Biot-Savart summation compiled by one compiler, the CuAD adjoint costs about four times the primal at every size, as does Enzyme when the source declares the absence of aliasing with __restrict__. On the unchanged source Enzyme caches the loop in the device heap and costs 9 to 240 times the primal, while the heap tape of Clad costs 60 to 4400 times the primal and fails beyond 8192 vortices. Exact Jacobians assembled from the generated tangents also matter for accuracy. In single precision, the adjoint gradient of a finite-difference Jacobian reaches errors of 45 to 75 per cent on a stiff Burgers problem and of $5\times10^{-4}$ to $4\times10^{-2}$ on a transonic airfoil, whereas the generated Jacobian keeps them below $5\times10^{-5}$ and $3\times10^{-6}$. The applications include the shape sensitivities of lift and drag of a transonic NACA 0012, for which the residual, the boundary conditions and the wall force are differentiated by CuAD and the adjoint agrees with the tangent to $10^{-13}$.
item.dc:creator: Seunghyun Joo

item.title: Resonant lunar tides of Earth's core and basal magma ocean
item.description: arXiv:2606.16340v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Earth's magnetic field is generated by fluid motion in the liquid-metal core and has been active for billions of years. However, prior to the onset of inner-core growth, the sources of mechanical power that drove the geodynamo remain uncertain. During this period, the core may have been overlain by a basal magma ocean (BMO), creating two immiscible fluid layers separated by a density interface, beneath the solid mantle. We develop a theory for lunar tides in this core--BMO system, in which the tidal potential acts on the density contrast between the two layers. The resulting dynamics differ fundamentally from previous models driven by imposed deformation of the core's bounding envelope. In the inviscid limit, the response transitions from an equilibrium tide to an interfacial gravity wave as forcing frequency increases. The two regimes are separated by a resonance that occurs when the forcing frequency matches the natural frequency of the degree-2, order-2 interfacial mode. The inviscid core flow is formally identical to the canonical elliptical vortex, linking the problem to the theory of elliptical instability. Finite viscosity regularises the resonance, introduces phase lag and generates oscillatory boundary layers. Combined with parameterised models of lunar recession and BMO crystallisation, the theory predicts enhanced core-boundary ellipticity, core-flow speed, magnetic Reynolds number and instability metrics, particularly near resonance. These results identify a previously unexplored mechanism for tidally driven flow in differentiated planetary bodies and show that a BMO can enhance tidal coupling to the core, potentially contributing to dynamo action.
item.dc:creator: Murray B. C. Kiernan, Hamish C. F. C. Hay, David W. Rees Jones, James F. J. Bryson, Richard F. Katz

item.title: Operator learning for efficient quantum computation
item.description: arXiv:2606.20184v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: An efficient implementation of quantum algorithms is often hindered by the lack of efficient primitives for operators and state preparation. This limits both the ability of near-term quantum hardware to simulate complex problems and the potential of fault-tolerant algorithms to achieve practical quantum advantage. To address this, we propose a framework that maps discrete operators onto compact, structured quantum circuits. The resulting variational circuits can be tailored to the connectivity and long-range interaction of the target hardware. The learning process employs backpropagation together with a cost function that efficiently optimizes unitary operators and non-unitary --dense or sparse-- operators using only a single ancilla qubit for block encoding. Additionally, we introduce a regularization term that reduces the approximation error. The approach is validated for both quantum mechanical and engineering applications. In the former case, we learn propagators that arise in native quantum problems --such as quantum simulation and quantum chemistry-- and achieve improved resource scaling in comparison to standard Suzuki--Trotter expansions. In the latter case, we demonstrate the approach's ability to implement the second-order central finite difference approximation of the Laplace operator --relevant for solving partial differential equations-- while improving upon current error metrics. The final example deals with learning a dense, non-unitary operator that arises in the analysis of inviscid potential flow around an airfoil. These results motivate the extension of the framework to a broader class of operator-synthesis problems beyond the prototypical engineering and quantum applications considered here.
